topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: Technological integration and professional competency development: a structural equation analysis of generative AI, learning engagement, and media literacy in journalism education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Technological integration and professional competency development: a structural equation analysis of generative AI, learning engagement, and media literacy in journalism education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on journalism education specifically; sample size and geographic scope unclear from snippet. Findings may not generalise beyond journalism programmes or to other professional disciplines.
takeaways: Structural equation modelling suggests that generative AI integration alone does not automatically improve professional competency — learning engagement and media literacy act as critical mediating factors. Ensure your AI literacy programme actively builds engagement and critical evaluation skills, not just tool exposure.

In journalism (and likely other media-adjacent roles), media literacy appears essential for safe and effective AI adoption. Assess whether your employees can evaluate AI-generated content critically before scaling AI tools in your organisation.
The research highlights the importance of positioning AI literacy within broader professional development frameworks rather than treating it as a standalone technical skill.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on higher education sector which may not directly translate to workplace AI literacy development. Generalisability to organisational settings depends on whether content addresses both academic and professional competency frameworks.
takeaways: Higher education strategies for AI competency development may include curriculum design, hands-on projects, and interdisciplinary approaches that could be adapted for employee upskilling programmes.
Identify which competencies emphasised in academic AI literacy (technical skills, critical thinking, ethical reasoning) are most transferable to your organisation's specific AI capabilities needs.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education context; applicability to corporate or other sectors depends on whether the four-domain model translates beyond academic management.
takeaways: Adopt a four-domain framework for AI literacy development (likely covering technical understanding, ethical awareness, strategic thinking, and practical application) rather than treating AI skills as isolated competencies.

Position AI literacy as a meta-skill that enables employees to learn and adapt across multiple roles, rather than a static technical skill — useful for planning upskilling programs in your organisation.
Use this model to design integrated AI literacy pathways for managers and leaders, ensuring they understand both the strategic and operational implications of AI adoption.

articles.title: US Department of Labor promotes AI literacy across the American workforce - U.S. Department of Labor (.gov)
articles.snippet: US Department of Labor promotes AI literacy across the American workforce  U.S. Department of Labor (.gov)
articles.generalisability: US-specific — describes US Department of Labor initiatives, funding schemes, and policy that do not apply in Australia. Findings may have limited relevance to Australian workforce development contexts.
takeaways: US-specific: The DoL's approach to scaling AI literacy highlights the policy levers available in the US (grants, workforce programmes) — Australian organisations should explore equivalent state and federal support through ASIC, NESA, and Skills Australia.

Systematic promotion of AI literacy at a national level signals that foundational AI competency is now a workforce priority — consider aligning internal upskilling programmes with emerging occupational standards.

Large-scale government backing for AI literacy suggests demand for accessible, non-technical training — explore whether your organisation's learning design matches workers' entry-level needs and prior experience.

articles.title: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students | Scientific Reports - Nature
articles.snippet: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students | Scientific Reports  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are limited to higher vocational education settings and may not generalise to corporate workplace learning contexts or other education levels. Geographic scope unclear from snippet provided.
takeaways: A validated competency ladder framework can structure AI literacy development in stages — consider mapping similar progressive pathways for your organisation's AI upskilling programs rather than treating AI literacy as a single competency.

Vocational education models emphasise practical competency validation — explore how workplace assessments of AI capability could be structured similarly, with clear milestones employees must demonstrate before advancing.

Competency-based pathways allow personalised progression — your literacy programs could identify where employees sit on a validated ladder and provide targeted development rather than one-size-fits-all training.

articles.title: The influence of employability skills on quality of employment in AI-driven labour market transformations: the roles of academic achievement and motivation - Nature
articles.snippet: The influence of employability skills on quality of employment in AI-driven labour market transformations: the roles of academic achievement and motivation  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unable to assess from title and snippet alone — geographic scope, sample size, and methodology are not indicated. Recommend reviewing full article for details on study design, participant demographics, and sector coverage.
takeaways: Focus on developing employability skills (communication, problem-solving, adaptability) as foundational preparation for AI-driven workforce transitions, not just technical AI competency.

Consider how academic achievement and employee motivation interact with skills development — motivation may be a critical lever for translating learning into quality employment outcomes in AI-transformed roles.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from the title and snippet alone. The approach-avoidance framework may apply across sectors, but findings could be limited by geographic scope, industry type, or organisational context.
takeaways: Use approach-avoidance theory to predict how employees will respond to AI implementation—some will proactively reshape their roles while others may withdraw or resist; tailor support and communication accordingly.

Monitor job crafting behaviours during AI adoption as an early indicator of employee engagement and psychological safety; employees actively reshaping their jobs suggest positive adaptation, while avoidance signals potential disengagement or anxiety that requires intervention.

articles.title: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior - Nature
articles.snippet: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not clear from title/snippet alone. Findings likely most applicable to cybersecurity professionals but may not extend broadly to non-technical roles or different organisational contexts.
takeaways: Building AI self-efficacy among cybersecurity staff may buffer against job stress and improve security behaviours — consider targeted upskilling programs to increase confidence in AI-assisted security tools.
Job stress appears to undermine cybersecurity compliance; interventions should address both workload/pressure and skill confidence to reduce risk of security lapses.

Psychological factors (stress, self-efficacy) directly shape security behaviour — HR and security teams should collaborate to design roles that manage uncertainty and build capability rather than relying solely on compliance training.

articles.title: Why Companies That Choose AI Augmentation Over Automation May Win in the Long Run - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why Companies That Choose AI Augmentation Over Automation May Win in the Long Run  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents strategic argument for AI augmentation vs automation but lacks empirical data or case studies. Applicability depends on industry sector and organisational maturity, not validated across different contexts.
takeaways: Consider positioning AI as a tool to enhance employee capabilities rather than replace them—this may improve retention, skill development, and long-term competitive advantage over pure automation strategies.

Organisations adopting augmentation approaches should invest in training employees to work effectively alongside AI systems, since the value comes from human-AI collaboration rather than displacement.
Evaluate your AI strategy against long-term workforce stability and capability-building goals, not just short-term cost reduction through automation.

articles.title: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full article — scope, sample size, and methodology not evident from title and snippet alone. Geographic location and sector coverage unknown.
takeaways: Psychological safety is a critical protective factor when implementing AI in your workplace — organisations that prioritise safe discussion about AI concerns and mistakes may mitigate depression and mental health impacts on workers.

Before deploying AI, audit whether your team feels psychologically safe to voice concerns about automation, job security, or capability gaps; low safety predicts worse psychological outcomes regardless of AI adoption itself.

articles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The focus on self-efficacy and transformational leadership as moderators suggests findings may apply across sectors, but geographic scope and sample size are unclear.
takeaways: Build employee self-efficacy proactively when implementing AI — workers with stronger self-efficacy experience less job insecurity during AI adoption, suggesting training and capability-building should precede or accompany technology rollout.

Model transformational leadership visibly during AI transitions — leaders who inspire confidence, articulate a compelling vision, and provide individualised support can significantly buffer employees' anxiety about AI-driven job changes.

Address job insecurity as a discrete concern during AI implementation rather than assuming it will resolve naturally — the moderating effects suggest targeted interventions on both individual (self-efficacy) and leadership (transformational style) can meaningfully reduce negative psychological outcomes.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet alone. Findings on psychological ownership and AI crafting may be particularly relevant in paternalistic leadership contexts (common in Asian organisations), but applicability to other leadership styles and Western organisational cultures requires examination of the full methodology.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership among employees by allowing them autonomy in how they adapt and personalise AI tools to their workflows ('AI crafting') — this appears to strengthen collaboration with AI systems.

Paternalistic leaders can leverage their position of trust and benevolent authority to encourage employees to take ownership of AI integration, rather than positioning AI adoption as top-down mandate.
Monitor whether employees feel genuine ownership of AI tools versus compliance; psychological ownership drives qualitatively different engagement than mandated use.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without clearly defined empirical scope or geographic boundaries. Findings and recommendations may reflect US academic/business context.
takeaways: Identify which specific work roles and tasks in your organisation are most likely to be augmented or displaced by AI, then design targeted upskilling programmes for affected employees before disruption occurs.
Create internal communication and change management processes that transparently address AI adoption timelines and retraining opportunities, reducing uncertainty-driven resistance to AI integration.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — sample characteristics, geographic scope, and sector details are not provided in the snippet; findings may not generalise across different organisational contexts or cultural settings.
takeaways: Understanding whether employees approach or avoid job crafting in response to AI adoption can help you design change management strategies that encourage proactive upskilling rather than defensive withdrawal.

Use this framework to assess your own team's response to AI tools — identify whether resistance stems from avoidance motivation and intervene with support, training, or role redesign to shift toward approach-oriented engagement.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on BCG's consulting experience across multiple sectors and regions, but specific case details and applicability may vary by organisation size, industry, and maturity level.
takeaways: Design AI adoption programmes that treat workforce capability development as central to transformation strategy, not an afterthought — include upskilling, role redesign, and change management from the outset.
Identify and engage 'AI champions' within teams early to model new ways of working and help peers overcome resistance, rather than relying solely on top-down directives.

Establish clear expectations about how AI will change daily work tasks and career paths, then provide transparent communication and targeted training to reduce anxiety and build confidence in new tools.

articles.title: Generative AI adoption and employee outcomes: a conservation of resources perspective on job crafting, career commitment, and the moderating role of liking of AI - Nature
articles.snippet: Generative AI adoption and employee outcomes: a conservation of resources perspective on job crafting, career commitment, and the moderating role of liking of AI  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings likely apply broadly to knowledge workers adopting AI tools, but generalisability depends on sample characteristics (sector, geography, organisational context) not evident from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Employee attitudes toward AI (liking/acceptance) matter as much as the technology itself — investing in building positive AI perceptions through training and change communication may be as important as the tool rollout.

Job crafting behaviours emerge as a key mechanism through which employees adapt to AI adoption — encourage and enable workers to reshape their roles and tasks to complement (rather than resist) new AI capabilities.
Career commitment may fluctuate during AI adoption; proactively address employee concerns about career trajectory and skill relevance to prevent disengagement during the transition period.

articles.title: Reconfiguring work: Change management in the age of gen AI - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Reconfiguring work: Change management in the age of gen AI  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey research typically draws on global client work and surveys, but findings may reflect practices in large, well-resourced organisations and may not fully represent small-to-medium enterprises or non-profit sectors.
takeaways: Identify and map which roles and workflows will be most affected by gen AI adoption, then prioritise change management efforts on those areas rather than attempting organisation-wide transformation simultaneously.

Design reskilling and transition pathways early in your change process — waiting until after AI implementation often creates resistance and demoralisation; communicate what new skills employees will need and how the organisation will support them.

Establish clear governance and decision-making structures for gen AI rollout, including who owns adoption, how success will be measured, and how employee feedback will be incorporated — ambiguity on these points is a leading cause of change fatigue.

articles.title: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample composition, which are not evident from the title and snippet alone. The focus on DEI interventions suggests potential relevance across sectors, but geographic scope and sample characteristics are unclear.
takeaways: Design AI systems and work processes with explicit attention to inclusive outcomes — DEI interventions are not add-ons but active moderators that shape how algorithmic systems affect different employee groups.

Cultivate a diversity-supportive organisational culture in parallel with AI implementation; culture acts as a buffer that determines whether algorithmic changes reduce or amplify existing inequities in the workplace.

Audit algorithmic work design for unintended disparate impact on underrepresented groups — inclusive design requires proactive testing and refinement, not passive hope that good intentions will translate to equitable outcomes.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — the snippet provides insufficient detail about the underlying study's sample size, geographic scope, methodology, or whether findings have been replicated. The sensationalised headline ('shocking difference') suggests popular science reporting rather than primary research.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies consistently find structural and functional differences in regions associated with empathy and impulse control in individuals with psychopathic traits — a counterintuitive finding given that psychopathy is often portrayed as purely behavioural or learned.

The gap between neuroscience findings and public understanding is huge: while brain differences are detectable, they don't explain behaviour the way Hollywood suggests, and most people with similar brain patterns aren't criminals.

This type of research fascinates us because it taps into our desire to find a biological 'villain marker' — but the reality is messier and more interesting than simple brain-behaviour cause-and-effect.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — likely limited to wine reviews in specific language(s) and platforms; generalisability to broader personality assessment depends on unreported methodological details.
takeaways: AI can detect personality traits from seemingly mundane consumer writing like wine reviews — suggesting our everyday language reveals more about who we are than we might realise.
Wine tasting vocabulary and preferences aren't just about taste: they're a window into personality patterns, which is a fun example of how niche hobbies betray deeper psychological traits.
This kind of analysis hints at AI's surprising ability to infer psychological characteristics from real-world behaviour and language that humans might miss or dismiss as just 'wine snobbery'.

articles.title: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Cannot assess from snippet alone — no methodological details provided. The link between thyroid function and personality traits is understudied; findings may be preliminary or from a limited sample.
takeaways: Your thyroid might be doing more than regulating metabolism — it could influence personality expression, suggesting the body's chemistry plays a surprising role in shaping how dark or light our traits appear.

This finding challenges the assumption that personality is purely psychological; it hints at unexpected biological mechanisms behind traits like narcissism or callousness that we usually think of as purely behavioural or learned.

articles.title: Gender Differences in Personality across the Ten Aspects of the Big Five - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Gender Differences in Personality across the Ten Aspects of the Big Five  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition and size, which are not detailed in the snippet provided. Large-scale personality studies often draw from diverse populations, but geographic scope and demographic representation are unclear.
takeaways: The Big Five personality model can be broken down into ten more granular aspects, revealing gender differences that don't appear at the broader trait level — suggesting we've been oversimplifying personality comparisons.
Personality differences between genders are more nuanced and multidimensional than popular stereotypes suggest, challenging the idea that men and women differ uniformly across all traits.
This kind of detailed personality mapping could help explain why broad gender generalisations often fail in practice — individuals vary enormously within their gender on specific aspects.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on twin study methodology and sample characteristics not detailed in the snippet; twin studies typically reflect populations where they were conducted but findings on heritability of political beliefs are subject to ongoing debate in behavioural genetics.
takeaways: Authoritarian political beliefs appear to have measurable genetic roots rather than being purely environmentally determined — a counterintuitive finding that challenges the assumption that political ideology is simply learned or chosen.

Twin study methodology can disentangle nature versus nurture contributions to abstract beliefs like authoritarianism, revealing that even complex social and political attitudes have biological substrates worth investigating.

The finding that genes influence political orientation invites fascinating questions about whether we inherit not just personality traits but also our fundamental instincts about power, order, and social hierarchy.

articles.title: Curiosity and surprise differentially affect memory depending on age - Nature
articles.snippet: Curiosity and surprise differentially affect memory depending on age  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings on age-related differences in how curiosity and surprise influence memory may have broad applicability across age groups, but generalisability depends on sample composition, which is not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Curiosity and surprise don't have the same memory-boosting effect for everyone — age matters in unexpected ways, suggesting our brains handle learning triggers differently as we grow older.
The counterintuitive insight that surprise and curiosity work independently on memory (rather than together) challenges common assumptions about what makes things stick in our minds.

This finding could explain why educational strategies and marketing approaches that rely on 'shock value' or 'creating curiosity' might land very differently depending on whether they're aimed at younger or older audiences.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad but potentially skewed toward PwC's client base and English-speaking respondents. Large sample size likely, but sector representation and geographic weighting not specified in snippet.
takeaways: Identify which specific workforce concerns (hopes/fears) are most prevalent in your organisation by comparing internal pulse survey data against PwC's global benchmarks to prioritise safety and culture interventions.

Use findings to shape psychological safety messaging — if job security or AI disruption fears feature prominently in global data, proactively address these anxieties through transparent communication and upskilling pathways.

Consider geographic and sector variation in the full report; concerns may differ significantly between regions and industries, requiring tailored safety initiatives rather than one-size-fits-all policies.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability is limited without access to full methodology — the title suggests a correlational study linking AI adoption to depression outcomes, but sample size, geographic scope, sectors covered, and causal inference strength cannot be assessed from the snippet alone.
takeaways: AI adoption can increase employee depression risk when psychological safety is low — prioritise building trust and open dialogue about AI implementation concerns before and during rollout, not after.

Ethical leadership is a protective factor during AI transitions — leaders must explicitly model and communicate ethical principles around AI use, demonstrate accountability for decisions, and create space for employees to raise concerns without fear of retaliation.

Monitor psychological safety metrics as a leading indicator of AI adoption risk — if safety scores drop during implementation, depression and disengagement are likely to follow; treat safety as a measurable prerequisite, not an afterthought.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG research typically draws on global consulting experience and client data, but specific sample characteristics, methodologies, and geographic representation are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Create explicit norms that invite diverse perspectives and questions without fear of ridicule or punishment; this reduces the likelihood that capable employees self-censor or disengage.
Leaders should model vulnerability and admit mistakes publicly — this signals that psychological safety is genuine, not just rhetorical, and encourages others to take interpersonal risks.

Measure psychological safety through pulse surveys or focus groups regularly; organisations that treat it as a measurable culture metric (not just a nice-to-have) are more likely to sustain it and close performance gaps linked to employee voice.

articles.title: Middle Managers Feel the Least Psychological Safety at Work - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Middle Managers Feel the Least Psychological Safety at Work  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — no sample size, methodology, or geographic scope details provided in the snippet. Generalisability cannot be assessed without access to the full article.
takeaways: Middle managers may be an overlooked vulnerability in psychological safety initiatives; audit whether your safety-building efforts reach this tier or inadvertently exclude them from peer support and voice opportunities.

If middle managers experience lower psychological safety, they are less likely to model safe behaviours or foster safety in teams they supervise — consider targeted interventions (peer groups, senior sponsor relationships) to break this cycle.

articles.title: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams - SHRM
articles.snippet: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams  SHRM
articles.generalisability: Moderate — SHRM content is US-focused and reflects US HR practices, though psychological safety principles are applicable across contexts. May reference US-specific employment law or HR frameworks.
takeaways: Identify and model the specific leader behaviours that signal safety (e.g., admitting mistakes, inviting dissent, responding non-defensively) so your team understands what psychological safety looks like in practice.
Implement a concrete mechanism to solicit and act visibly on team feedback—such as regular pulse surveys or retrospectives—then close the loop by showing how input shaped decisions.
Establish clear norms about how mistakes and failures are discussed, ensuring they are treated as learning opportunities rather than threats to job security.

articles.title: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams - Deloitte
articles.snippet: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Limited — Deloitte report with no detail on sample composition, geography, or methodology in the snippet provided. Findings likely reflect Deloitte's client base (predominantly large, multinational organisations) and may not generalise to SMEs or non-Western contexts.
takeaways: Psychological safety underpins team performance — prioritise creating conditions where team members feel safe to speak up, take interpersonal risks, and admit mistakes without fear of embarrassment or retaliation.
Assess your team's current capability gaps (technical, collaborative, adaptive) and design targeted development interventions rather than assuming all high performers have the same strengths.
Build feedback loops into team processes so that capability needs are surfaced regularly and addressed early, preventing performance plateaus.
